previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A young woman with a history of congenital tracheomalacia, bronchomalacia, tracheostomy, and chronic respiratory colonization with MRSA and Pseudomonas was admitted for worsening cough, neck pain, odynophagia, and green tracheal discharge. Initial evaluation revealed tenderness and swelling at the trach site, but imaging showed only mild laryngeal edema without abscess, and labs showed no leukocytosis. Sputum and bronchial cultures grew MRSA and Pseudomonas, but minimal inflammatory cells suggested colonization rather than active infection. Antibiotics were discontinued after infectious disease consultation. Pain was managed with IV morphine initially, then transitioned to oral oxycodone and tramadol. The trach tube was replaced by interventional pulmonology, and ENT confirmed no tracheitis. Supportive care included hypertonic saline nebulizers, bronchodilators, and saline drops via trach. She was discharged home with instructions to use a heat-moisture exchanger during the day, humidified air at night, and scheduled saline drops, along with follow-up with pulmonary and ENT specialists.

Brief Hospital Course:
This is a ___ year old female with chronic trach, recently 
admitted on ___ with neck pain now re-presenting to ___ ED 
after being called back for positive blood cultures (initially 
coag negative staph). She was found to have high-grade 
Staphylococcus LUG___ bacteremia. 

#High-grade Staphylococcus LUG___ bacteremia. This bacteria 
can be a skin contaminant, however, she had multiple subsequent 
positive blood cultures. Possible portals of entry to the 
bloodstream include trach and port. Her port/tracheostomy site 
did not appear to be infected. She did have a tiny abscess under 
left axilla, aspirate of which grew MRSA, suggesting that this 
was not the source. TTE revealed no endocarditis. ID was 
consulted for assistance with treatment. In an attempt to 
salvage port, she was treated with both IV vancomycin and 
vancomycin dwells. She well need at least 4 weeks of both. 

#Chronic sore throat, cough, chest pain of atypical etiology: Pt 
has had these complaints nearly every admission. CT neck did not 
show abnormalities and EKGs were normal. Oropharynx appeared 
within normal limits. She continued home oxycodone and tramadol. 
She did complete a 3 day course of toradol and lidocaine patch 
with partial relief. 

#Hidradenitis suppurativa: Pt found to have moderately sized, 
tender abscess under left axilla. Given bacteremia, this was a 
suspected source. Aspirate grew MRSA, however. ACS did not drain 
this abscess, as this is relatively contraindicated in this 
disease. She was given clindamycin ointment and IV vancomycin 
(for bacteremia as above). 

#Anemia: H/H were relatively stable. Ferritin was 14. She would 
benefit from IV iron possibly. 

CHRONIC ISSUES: 
# S/p trach: She continued saline/duonebs. Seen by ENT with no 
acute processes noted. 
# Depression: She continued home fluoxetine.  
# GERD: She continued home ranitidine and omeprazole.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms ___,

It was a pleasure taking care of you at the ___ 
___. You were admitted for bacteria that 
grew in blood cultures from your previous ED visit. 

You had several new blood cultures grow bacteria, which we think 
may be from your skin. You are at risk for this given your 
tracheostomy and port. 

We treated you with intravenous vancomycin and vancomycin locks, 
which keep vancomycin in port when you are not using it. 

You will need these antibiotics for at least 4 weeks. Your labs 
will need to be drawn at least once weekly to make sure the 
levels of antibiotic are high enough. 

You also complained of chest and throat pain, as well as cough. 
We found to new infection or other cause that could be 
contributing to this. You continued your home medications and we 
also gave you a lidocaine patch to put on your chest, which 
helped somewhat. 

You were also found to have a small abscess in your left 
underarm. Some of the fluid was aspirated with a needle. It did 
not grow the same bacteria as the bacteria in your blood, so it 
is not the source. Your intravenous antibiotic should be 
treating it, and we also gave you a new prescription for an 
antibiotic lotion called clindamycin for you to use at home. 

You should follow-up with the appointments listed below. 

On behalf of your ___ team,
We wish you all the best
